1:
The second session of the heavenly council opens the chapter, and the witnesses meet it on two fronts at once — the mystery of why the accuser is admitted a second time, and the length of the interval since the first. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great sees in the renewed assault the very measure of Job's growth: blessed Job, though aimed at for death in his temptation, gained growth unto life by the stroke, and the old enemy grieved to find that he had only multiplied the saint's excellences by the means by which he had thought to do them away. Beaten in the first struggle, Satan yet girds himself for fresh assaults of temptations, still bold to augur evil of a holy man — for one who is himself evil can never believe goodness to exist, though his own experience prove it. Gregory even hears a difference in the familiar question: when the Lord asks "Whence comest thou?" it cannot, he thinks, be addressed to Satan just as it was before, for now the accuser returns defeated from the very contest upon which he had been let loose.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene as a court reconvened. Satan, that sworn enemy to God and all good men, is here pushing forward his malicious prosecution of Job, whom he hates because God loves him. One would have thought he had enough of his former defeat; but malice is restless. He comes not to confess his mistake and beg pardon, but with a further design; and, asked the same question as before, he answers as before — "from going to and fro in the earth" — as if he had been doing no harm at all. Henry hears in this the accuser of the brethren who, as Rev. 12:10 says, accuses them before our God day and night, still urging that against them which has been many a time answered.

On the timing the witnesses divide. The reformed John Gill, taking the "sons of God" as good men and professors of religion met by agreement to worship, reckons the space since the former meeting short — a few days, a week or a fortnight at most — and rejects the Targum's notion of a whole year (the day of the great judgment at the year's beginning), since Satan would never grant Job so much breathing-time, nor would his friends have waited so long before they visited. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans the other way: how long after the first trial we cannot say, but probably one whole year, when, as the Targum intimates, it was the season of the annual atonement — time enough for Job's patience and resignation to have their scope. Clarke adds that the whole appearance is to be read metaphorically, teaching the existence of good and evil spirits, and that Satan can do no man hurt, in person or in property, but by God's express permission, which God grants only when he means to overrule it for his own greater glory and his servant's greater good. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott closes with a philological touch: "And Satan came also" recalls Job 1:7, and Peter applies to the adversary the very verb from which we have "peripatetic," the restless walker to and fro.
2:
"And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou?" — the question that had opened the first council is put a second time, and with only two witnesses at hand the reading stays close to the grammar, yet finds in the repetition more than a mere echo. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the same question is put to Satan and the same answer returned by him: he presents himself again among the sons of God, and gives once more the restless reply that he comes "from going to and fro in the earth," as though nothing had passed since his first defeat.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look closer and find one telling difference. The clause that states the purpose of the appearing, which at the first council had been said only of the sons of God, is here repeated in connection with Satan himself — for this time he comes with a most definite object in view, a fixed design against the man God had praised. Jehovah addresses him exactly as before; but the very word for "whence" is subtly varied from what Job 1:7 had used. Such small variations, Keil and Delitzsch observe, are frequent in Scripture's repetitions — as the Psalms will vary a returning refrain, or as the opening chapter itself interchanged two words for "still" and "yet" — and are not to be pressed as though they hid some change of meaning. After Satan's general answer, they add, Jehovah proceeds to inquire more particularly, and the second interrogation of the accuser begins.

Brief as the notice is, the two readings converge on what the doubled scene discloses. The accuser is not content with a single defeat; he returns to the same place, answers in the same wandering terms, and stands again where the sons of God present themselves — but this time, as Keil and Delitzsch stress, with a particular and settled malice against the one man God had commended. That the Lord again opens the interview with "Whence comest thou?" keeps the initiative where it belongs: Satan does not seize the floor but is summoned to give account of his roamings. The repetition is therefore not idle. It shows an enemy whose hatred is tireless and a God who governs even the accuser's approach, drawing him out to be questioned before ever a word of fresh temptation can be spoken. The stage is set a second time; and the reader who saw how the first council ended in Job's stripping is braced to see this one issue in a heavier stroke still.
3:
The Lord renews his testimony to Job, and the witnesses notice that the commendation is not merely repeated but enlarged. The reformed John Gill marks the addition: the same character is given as before — a perfect and upright man, one that feareth God and escheweth evil — but now continued and confirmed, with something added; for Job was no loser but a gainer in his character by his afflictions and trials, the very assault meant to strip him having only heightened his praise.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix on the logic of the sentence. From the fact that amid all his sufferings hitherto Job has preserved and proved his integrity — a term that, outside this book, occurs only in Proverbs 11:3 — the narrative draws its conclusion: there was no previous reason for the injury which Satan had urged God to decree. They are careful about the verb "movedst": it does not mean, as Umbreit thought, to lead astray, which would be an almost blasphemous anthropomorphism, but to instigate or incite, generally to evil, as at 1 Chron. 21:1 — the accuser had provoked the trial, but the ground of it lay in Satan, not in Job.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses guard the same point against a crude literalism. John Wesley glosses the "still" as meaning that Job holds fast notwithstanding all his afflictions and Satan's suggestion to the contrary; and the "movedst," he insists, like the rest of this representation, is not to be understood literally, but is meant to signify both the devil's restless malice in promoting man's misery and God's permission of it for wise and holy ends. Adam Clarke weighs the terrible phrase "to destroy him without cause": thou wouldst have me permit thee to destroy a man whose sins have not called for so heavy a judgment. He traces the original word, which signifies to swallow down or devour, to the very image Peter had in view when he warned that the adversary goeth about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, in 1 Peter 5:8.

The voices do not divide. Together they hold two truths that the verse will not let fall apart: that the affliction is real and severe, decreed by God's own permission, and yet "without cause" so far as Job is concerned — no guilt in the sufferer drew it down. The trial is not punishment but proof; and the God who allows the roaring lion his hour does so, as Wesley says, for ends wise and holy, that the integrity he commends may be displayed the brighter for being tried. What Satan meant to expose as hollow, the Lord holds up as sound; and the same suffering that the accuser reads as a lever to break Job, God reads as the seal of a servant who fears him for nothing.
4:
Satan answers God's commendation with a sneer that has become proverbial — "Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life" — and the witnesses gather to expose the slander folded into it. The reformed John Gill hears the accuser still refusing to own Job as the man God had described, insinuating instead that he is selfish and mercenary, and that the trial has not been pushed far or close enough to discover him: he has lost his substance, his servants, his children, but he keeps his own life, his health and ease, and so long as he enjoys these he will serve God — but only for their sake.

The wesleyan-arminian voices spell out the malice. Adam Clarke takes "skin for skin" to mean that a man will part with all he has, piecemeal, to save his life, giving up limb after limb so long as there is hope that by such sacrifices life may be spared — the sense, he judges, given by the Targum, and the reason the Lord will presently say "save his life." John Wesley presses the insinuation home: this patience of Job's, Satan means, is no evidence of sincere and generous piety but a mere act of self-love; he is content to lose estate and children while he sleeps in a whole skin, and it is not true patience but policy, that he may appease God's wrath and prevent further plagues upon his own carcase. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it as a more extreme form of the first insinuation of Job 1:9: Job takes care to have his quid pro quo, and if the worst come to the worst will give up everything to save his life; his service, on this telling, is worth no more than that selfish object implies.

The other grammatical-historical witnesses turn to the knot in the phrase itself. Keil and Delitzsch survey the proposals and set them aside one by one — Olshausen's idea that Job will leave Jehovah untouched so long as his own skin is spared, which even in the devil's mouth is too unbecomingly put; Hupfeld's "skin" of cattle and servants and children bartered so Job may get off with his own skin sound; the common "like for like" of Hirzig and Ewald, which rests on the strange claim that one skin is much like another. Against all these they hold to the plain and cutting sense the other witnesses share.

The witnesses do not divide on the substance. Whatever the precise turn of the proverb, its thrust is one — the accuser cannot conceive of a disinterested goodness, and so reduces the piety he cannot deny to a bare calculation of self-preservation. It is the same lie he told at the first council, now sharpened: that no man, not even Job, fears God for nothing, and that let a man's own flesh be threatened, and his religion will be seen for the bargain it always was. The verse thus lays down the terms of the second trial before ever a boil appears — not whether Job will lose more, but whether, when the loss reaches his own body, his fear of God will hold.
5:
Having reduced Job's piety to self-love, Satan names the one blow he thinks will break it — "put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh." The reformed John Gill reads the demand as the motion for a second trial: the accuser asks God to take off the hand of providence that had secured Job's health, and to stretch out instead a hand of power that would fill his flesh with diseases and his bones with rottenness, touching him to the quick, to the very marrow where pain is sharpest — or, he allows, "his bone and his flesh" may simply stand for the man himself.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to what the permission will mean. Job has not forfeited his life; leave is given to place it in extreme peril and nothing more, that it may be seen whether, in the very face of death, he will deny the God who has decreed such heavy affliction. They are precise about the word for "life": it is not the same as the ordinary term for bodily existence, but denotes the soul that produces the spirit-life of man — though "life" must serve as the rendering, since we do not use "soul" in that sense.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the sting in Satan's prediction, "he will curse thee to thy face." The Hebrew, he notes, runs literally "if he will not bless thee to thy face" — a veiled form whose real meaning is a curse; and the accuser's whole wager is that Job's piety toward God will always be regulated by God's bounty toward Job, so that let the bounty be withdrawn and turned to pain, and the piety will turn to blasphemy.

The three witnesses converge on the terrible confidence of the challenge. Satan does not ask to kill Job outright; he asks to make him wish for death, to lodge the affliction in Job's own bone and flesh where he cannot flee it, certain that bodily anguish will accomplish what the loss of goods and children could not. Gill's reading of the request, Keil and Delitzsch's care over the imperilled but guarded life, and Clarke's exposure of the veiled curse all serve one point: the second trial is aimed not at Job's estate but at his person, and its whole design is to prove the accuser's thesis that a man in torment will let go his integrity and arraign his God. The verse leaves the wager laid down, and the reader waiting to see whether flesh and bone can hold what wealth and family could not shake.
6:
God grants the trial, but with a chain on it — "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life" — and the witnesses dwell on both the astonishing permission and the strict limit set upon it. The reformed John Gill lingers over the "behold": well may a note of wonder be prefixed, that a saint and servant of God should be suffered to come into the hand of Satan. Yet it must not be misread, as though Job were now off God's heart, or out of God's keeping, or become the devil's property and child; none of these can be true of a good man, for nothing can separate him from the love of God — not Satan with all his principalities and powers — nor can any pluck him from the hand of God or of his Son, nor can a child of God be a child of the devil the next day, whatever some men's divinity may suppose.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marvels at the paradox of the proviso, "but save his life." Satan may afflict the body, but against the life he shall have no power; the word, Clarke notes, might be rendered "keep his soul," yet it also means life — and so, astonishingly, the very life of this holy man is placed in the hands of the destroyer. How wonderful the economy of salvation, that by God's unlimited power and skill the grand adversary of souls is made, by God's own order, the preserver of that which the evil of his nature incessantly prompts him to destroy. John Wesley reads the same limit as pure mercy: if God did not chain up the roaring lion, how soon would he devour us; as far as he permits the wrath of Satan and of wicked men to proceed against his people, he will make it turn to his praise and theirs, and the remainder he will restrain.

Wesley draws the type out further: Job, thus maligned by Satan, was a figure of Christ, whose heel the enemy had leave to bruise, whose bone and flesh — yea, and whose life also — he was suffered to touch; for by dying Christ would do what Job could not, and destroy him that had the power of death. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott grounds the whole scene in a steadier confidence: God's faithfulness cannot fail even if, as Satan hints, Job's should — as 2 Timothy 2:13 declares — and there was One who cared for Job's life more than Job cared for it himself. The witnesses do not divide. They hold together the daring truth that God hands his servant to the enemy, and the saving truth that he keeps the enemy on a leash: the life is spared, the love is unbroken, and the very malice let loose is bent, unwilling, to serve God's own purpose.
7:
Satan goes forth with his enlarged commission and strikes, and the witnesses turn from the council chamber to the ash-heap, dividing chiefly over the nature of the disease. The reformed John Gill marks only that the accuser, having got his leave, departed at once, eager to put his malice in execution. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees the tempter change his office: having worried Job as a persecutor, he now falls to work as a tormentor, smiting him with sore boils from head to foot, an evil inflammation as if set on fire of hell. One boil in the gathering is torment enough; what a case was Job's, covered all over, no part free, able to lie down no way for any ease. Henry draws the sober lesson that we know not how much Satan may have a hand, by divine permission, in the diseases that afflict the children of men — what infections that prince of the air may spread, what inflammations may come from that fiery serpent — remembering the woman whom Satan had bound eighteen years in Luke 13:16.

On the name of the malady the grammatical-historical witnesses speak with one voice. Keil and Delitzsch identify it, from the symptoms named later in the book, as elephantiasis — the most fearful form of leprosy, in which the limbs become jointless lumps like an elephant's legs — a disease that spares not even the higher ranks, as it seized Baldwin, king of Jerusalem; and they hear behind it the language of the covenant curses of Deut. 28:35. Charles Ellicott agrees: the "sore boils" are supposed to be elephantiasis, an extreme form of leprosy in which the skin becomes clotted and hard like an elephant's, with painful cracks and sores beneath.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is less sure, and lays the alternatives side by side. The disorder, he grants, may be the leprosy — which would explain why Job dwelt apart in an unclean place, and why his friends beheld him afar off, the disease being reckoned infectious. But the scraping with a potsherd argues an intolerable itching, one of the marks of the smallpox; and Clarke queries whether that was not rather the disease, noting that in leprosy and elephantiasis the whole surface is one uniform disordered mass, whereas in smallpox each pustule is a separate inflammation, with raging fever and intolerable anguish. John Wesley keeps to the plain biblical echo: the boils were like those inflicted on the Egyptians, called by the same word and threatened against apostate Israel in Deut. 28:27, making Job loathsome to himself and to his nearest kin, with consuming pain in the body and no less anguish in the mind. So the witnesses agree on the horror and differ only on the diagnosis — leprous elephantiasis, say Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott; perhaps rather the smallpox, queries Clarke — while all confess that whatever its medical name, the stroke reached from the sole of the foot to the crown, and left the man of God with nothing whole about him but his integrity.
8:
The stricken man is shown to us tending his own sores, and the witnesses read the two small actions of the verse — the potsherd and the ashes — as a picture of patience in the depths. The reformed John Gill first hears what the verse does not say: no murmuring, no repining, much less any cursing of God, came from Job's lips; he bore it all with the utmost patience, and took a piece of a broken pot, likely lying in the ashes about him, to scrape away the purulent matter that ran from his boils. He had no surgeon to mollify his ulcers with ointment or lay on healing plasters; his maids and servants, and even his wife, stood off at some distance, the smell of him grown well-nigh intolerable, so that he was left to do for himself what none would do for him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the sheer destitution of it. Instead of healing salves, a potsherd; and though a man sick and sore may bear it the better if he be well tended, Job has no such tending. Nothing is done for his running sores but what he does with his own hand; his children and servants are dead, his wife unkind, and none of those he had once befriended has the honour or gratitude to wipe his wounds — whether from loathing or fear of infection — so that here, as in the last days, men are lovers of their own selves, unthankful, and without natural affection. He has no fit instrument but a shard that would rather rake his wounds than ease them, and can only scrape them by wholesale, a remedy near as bad as the disease.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same details as tokens of humiliation. Job scraped himself not with soft linen — he had not enough of it now, or must have begged the help of those who abhorred to come near — nor with his own fingers, themselves ulcerous and unfit, but with potsherds, either as nearest at hand or as a sign of his deep humbling under God's hand, declining all that savoured of tenderness and delicacy. And the sitting is of a piece with it: the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply note that he sat down among the ashes, while Wesley and Henry find in it the posture of a mourner and a penitent, abasing himself in dust. "If God lay him among the ashes," Wesley says, "there he will contentedly sit down" — for a low spirit becomes low circumstances, and helps to reconcile us to them. The witnesses do not divide; they leave us the image of a great man seated in the ash-heap, scraping his sores with a broken shard, and yet, in all that misery, still holding his peace before God, so that the silence of the sufferer is itself the first answer to the accuser's wager.
9:
Into that silence comes the one voice most able to wound him, and the witnesses divide sharply over the woman who speaks and the words she uses. The reformed John Gill is inclined to think well of her: polygamy had not yet come in, Job had but one wife, and very probably she is the same who afterward bore him ten more children; she may have been a good woman for anything that appears, now in the dark about this providence and herself under a sore temptation. The Jewish fancy, carried by the Targum, that she was Dinah the daughter of Jacob, he thinks unlikely.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads her far more darkly, as Satan's spared instrument. She was left to Job when all else was taken, precisely to be a troubler and a tempter, for it is the devil's policy to send his temptations by the hand of those who are dear to us, as he tempted Adam by Eve and Christ by Peter. She banters Job for his constancy — "Dost thou still retain thine integrity?" — as if his religion were mere obstinacy toward a God who takes pleasure in his misery; and then she urges the blackest of counsels, to renounce God, blaspheme him, and end his troubles by ending his life. Nothing is more contrary to natural conscience than blaspheming God, nor to natural sense than self-murder, and the suggestion of either may well be suspected to come immediately from Satan.

On the very words the witnesses part. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take "renounce God, and die" to mean, as Job's own answer shows, to take leave of God — she counsels him to do the very thing Satan had boasted he would accomplish; yet they add, with Hengstenberg, that her desperation may proceed from strong love for her husband rather than from mere malice. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses hear the phrase as bitter irony. Adam Clarke, noting how the Septuagint swells her speech into a long lament, holds that the Hebrew verb rendered "curse" is really "bless," and that she speaks a savage sarcasm — "Bless God, and die!": bless him for his goodness while he destroys all thou hast, bless him for his support while he casts thee down. John Wesley reads the same edge — go on blessing God for thy losses and thy loathsome disease, and see how he rewards thee, and so bless God, and die as a fool dieth. The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, stands with Henry on the pain of it: thus a man's foes are they of his own household, as Micah 7:6 and Matthew 10:36 warn, and the worst trial of all is when those nearest us, instead of strengthening our hand in God, conspire to destroy our faith. So the witnesses leave two questions open — whether the wife spoke as Satan's mouthpiece or out of a love broken by grief, and whether her words were an open curse or a scalding irony — but they agree on the deadliness of the moment: the tempter had found the surest hand to carry his poison.
10:
Job's reply is the hinge of the whole trial, and the witnesses crowd round both his rebuke and his reasoning. The reformed John Gill is careful with the rebuke: Job does not call his wife a foolish woman, but says she speaks "as one of" them — the wicked and profane of that age — which intimates that she was herself a good woman now speaking out of character, like the carnal, or like the heathen who cast off their gods when crossed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the Hebrew: the word is stronger than "foolish woman," for it names one who thinks madly and acts impiously — "as one of the ungodly would speak, thou speakest" — yet the softening "one of" keeps the answer strong without being harsh.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole scene as a temptation resisted. Job is angry and sins not, taking the suggestion to curse God as the greatest of affronts, a very "Get thee behind me, Satan"; he does not rail at his wife as a man sick and sore might, but shows her the evil of what she said, that she spoke the language of the infidel. And his argument, Henry says, is unanswerable: good and evil are contraries, but they do not come from contrary causes; both are from the hand of God, and in both our eye must be up to him — thankful for the good, unfretting under the evil. To "receive" evil is to take it as a gift, neither despising the chastening nor fainting under it. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses turn it into a searching self-examination. Adam Clarke: shall we, who have had the long and unmerited use of God's blessings — which were never ours but only lent — be offended when the Owner comes to reclaim his own? John Wesley: shall we poor worms give laws to our supreme Lord and forbid him ever to afflict us, when his manifold past mercies so far outweigh these short corrections, and when the affliction itself may be a good for the soul, making us partakers of his holiness? Let murmuring, both agree, as well as boasting, be for ever excluded.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, finds Job's words wiser than Job knew: merely to receive evil as from God's hand transmutes its whole character, for then even calamities become blessings in disguise — a lesson Job was still learning, and one that sets his trial in sublime contrast with the temptation of Christ in Matthew 26:39-42 and the obedience learned through suffering in Hebrews 5:8. On the closing verdict — "in all this did not Job sin with his lips" — the witnesses stand together, though Clarke marks the Chaldee's careful qualification, that if Job sinned not with his lips, he may yet have thought hard words in his heart; and Henry allows there might have been risings of corruption within, but grace kept the upper hand, so that the man who offends not in word is, in this at least, a perfect man. Together the voices make the verse the answer to Satan's wager: the flesh is broken, the wife has turned tempter, and still the sufferer will receive both good and evil from the one hand of God.
11:
The scene widens from the ash-heap to the roads along which help is coming, as three friends set out to Job, and the witnesses attend both to who they were and to what their coming meant. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn in the story: after the sixth temptation comes a seventh, and now the real conflict begins, through which the hero of the book will pass — not indeed without sinning, yet still triumphantly. They place the men by their homes: Eliphaz from Teman, an old Idumaean name and a district celebrated for native wisdom, as Jeremiah 49:7 attests; Bildad from Shuah; Zophar from Naamah.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian commentators fill in the genealogy and the geography. Adam Clarke traces Eliphaz the Temanite to a son of Esau, and Teman to a city of Edom celebrated for wisdom — "Is wisdom no more in Teman?" — with Bildad the Shuhite sprung from Shuah, Abraham's son by Keturah, and Zophar the Naamathite from a Naamah bordering the Edomites; all of which, he argues, shows that Job dwelt in the land of Edom and his friends in Arabia Petraea nearby, and that the very sayings which follow prove their reputation for wisdom well founded. John Wesley agrees that they were men eminent for birth and quality, for knowledge, and for the profession of the true religion, probably of the posterity of Abraham; and he finds it a happy presage of God's grace to the Gentiles that so much wisdom and piety was preserved among those who were not children of the promise. Charles Ellicott adds the chronological hint — that Eliphaz's descent from Esau may roughly date the book — while confessing that of the district of Zophar the Naamathite nothing certain is known.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns from their pedigree to their friendship. A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity; these three had loved Job in his prosperity not for his feasts but for his pious converse, and now come to share his griefs as once they shared his comforts, for their heart was in the house of mourning. Henry notes that they came unbidden, made an appointment together to come, and set out with a sincere design to mourn with him and to comfort him — good people should so bind one another to good works — and yet, through their unskilful handling of his case, proved in the end but miserable comforters, so that many who aim well come short of their aim. Visiting the afflicted, he reminds us, is a branch of pure religion and undefiled. The witnesses do not divide: they show us wise and godly men, strangers to the covenant of promise yet rich in its fruits, who loved their friend enough to travel to his dunghill — even if the comfort they brought would prove, for many chapters yet, no comfort at all.
12:
The friends' first sight of Job undoes them, and the witnesses read their violent grief as the measure of how far he had fallen. The reformed John Gill pictures the moment of recognition failing — whether they were still at some distance from the house, Job sitting out in the open air, or were entering and saw him at the far part of the room. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the point plain and terrible: they lifted up their eyes afar off and knew him not; they saw a form that seemed to be Job but in which they could not recognize their friend. Then they weep, and rend their outer garments, and catch up dust to throw toward heaven that it may fall again upon their heads — the casting of dust on high being, they observe, the outward sign of an intense suffering that cries to heaven itself.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets these gestures in their wider human context, having often noted how the ancients expressed profound grief — wrapping themselves in sackcloth, covering the face, strewing dust or ashes on the head, sitting on the bare ground — significant actions in use among all nations, so that the friends mourn Job in the universal language of sorrow. The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, catches a poignant contrast in the words "knew him not," setting them against the love that could know a lost son under a disguise as great as Job's, or greater — the father who in Luke 15:20 recognized his boy while yet a great way off.

The witnesses do not divide, and the pathos of the verse gathers in that failure of recognition. Here were men who had known Job in the fulness of his greatness, and now, at a distance, their eyes refuse the evidence — the disease has so marred him that the friend is lost in the sufferer. Their tears, their torn robes, the dust flung heavenward and falling back upon their own heads, are not empty ceremony but the honest overflow of hearts appalled; and Keil and Delitzsch's note that the flung dust is grief crying to heaven gives the scene its true direction, for the friends' sorrow reaches instinctively upward, toward the God whose hand they feel behind so strange a ruin. They had come to comfort, and their first act is to be struck dumb with weeping at a change they can scarcely believe. Before ever a word is spoken, the depth of Job's affliction is measured for us in the speechless grief of those who loved him and could not, at first, so much as know his face.
13:
The chapter closes in a long silence, and the witnesses weigh both the custom behind it and the reasons the friends held their peace. The reformed John Gill explains the seven days and seven nights as the usual term of mourning — not that they sat the whole while without sleep or food, but that they came and sat the greater part of each of those days and nights, conforming themselves to Job and sympathizing with him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confirms the period from Scripture: Israel mourned seven days for Jacob in Genesis 50:10, the men of Jabesh seven days for Saul in 1 Samuel 31:13, and Ezekiel sat stunned seven days among the captives in Ezekiel 3:15 — so calamitous was Job's state that they treated him as already dead, and kept for him the mourning of the dead. John Wesley reads it the same way: seven days was the wonted mourning for the departed, fit for Job's children and for Job himself, who was in a manner dead while he lived.

Why they said nothing is the deeper question, and here the readings diverge. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reject the notion that mere custom or propriety prescribed the silence: it was rather the sheer force of the impression made upon them, and the fear of annoying the sufferer, that stopped their mouths — their feeling overpowered by reflection, their sympathy by dismay; and their long speechlessness betrays that they had not fully realized the purpose of their visit. It was a pity, they add, that they let Job utter the first word, which a kindly word of solace might have prevented; for it was in becoming fully conscious of his changed condition from their very silence that he broke forth at last with curses. Clarke and Wesley add a graver motive: they believed Job to be suffering for some heavy secret crime, and, seeing his anguish, would not add to it by reproach; the greatness of his misery, and the hand of God they perceived in it, made them question his sincerity even as they mourned, so that they knew not what to say and were loth to grieve him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lifts the eye from the friends to the writing itself: there is a colossal grandeur about this description, in keeping with the majesty and hoary antiquity of the poem. The witnesses do not finally divide — some laying the silence to overwhelming grief and dread, others to a suspicion they dared not voice, and Wesley owning both — but they leave the chapter poised on a knife-edge. Seven days the comforters sit dumb upon the ground, and their very silence, meant in kindness, presses upon Job until the pent grief must speak. So the narrative frame of the book closes, with the man stripped, smitten, tempted, and mourned as one dead, yet still not sinning; and the great debate is about to open, its first word left, ominously, to the sufferer himself.
